title: The THESAN-ZOOM project: clumpiness of high-redshift galaxies and its connection to bursty star formation
comment: 15 pages, 9 figures. Submitted to MNRAS. Comments are welcome!
summary: Recent JWST observations have revealed diverse high-redshift galaxy morphologies, including a population with irregular and clumpy structures. The physical origin of these structures, and the extent to which observational biases shape their appearance, remain uncertain. We present a power-spectrum-based method for quantifying galaxy clumpiness across spatial scales, using the radiation-hydrodynamic simulation suite THESAN-ZOOM, which employs a state-of-the-art galaxy formation model that resolves the multiphase interstellar medium (ISM). Although the total stellar mass distributions in THESAN-ZOOM galaxies are usually smooth, clumpy structures appear in the H$α$, far-ultraviolet (FUV), and optical light distributions. Tracers sensitive to shorter-timescale star formation exhibit more pronounced small-scale structure ($\sim10^{2}$--$10^{3}{\rm pc}$). The corresponding projected light spectra follow $P(k)\propto k^{-1}$ to $k^{-2}$, with progressively shallower slopes for tracers sensitive to more recent star formation, reflecting enhanced small-scale power and greater spatial intermittency in young stellar populations. This behaviour is consistent with a highly compressible, shock-dominated ISM in which stellar feedback and outflows reorganise dense gas into filamentary and clumpy structures. We also find that galaxy clumpiness depends on the treatment of stellar feedback. Weaker early stellar feedback enhances small-scale power in both the mass and light distributions. Clumpiness also varies strongly over the bursty star formation cycle, implying that observed samples may be biased towards galaxies caught in phases of elevated star formation. Galaxy clumpiness, therefore, could provide a complementary probe of the bursty star formation in the early Universe.

AI.tldr: The paper uses a power-spectrum-based method to quantify galaxy clumpiness across spatial scales using the THESAN-ZOOM radiation-hydrodynamic simulation suite. While stellar mass distributions are smooth, clumpy structures appear in Hα, FUV, and optical light distributions, with power spectra following P(k)∝k^-1 to k^-2. Clumpiness depends on stellar feedback treatment and varies strongly over the bursty star formation cycle, suggesting it could serve as a complementary probe of bursty star formation in the early Universe.
AI.motivation: Recent JWST observations have revealed diverse high-redshift galaxy morphologies, including irregular and clumpy structures, but the physical origin of these structures and the extent to which observational biases shape their appearance remain uncertain.
AI.method: The authors employ a power-spectrum-based approach to quantify galaxy clumpiness across spatial scales, applied to the THESAN-ZOOM simulation suite, which uses a state-of-the-art galaxy formation model resolving the multiphase interstellar medium (ISM).
AI.result: Tracers sensitive to shorter-timescale star formation exhibit more pronounced small-scale structure (~10^2-10^3 pc). Projected light spectra follow P(k)∝k^-1 to k^-2, with shallower slopes for tracers of more recent star formation. Galaxy clumpiness depends on stellar feedback treatment, with weaker early feedback enhancing small-scale power, and varies strongly over the bursty star formation cycle.
AI.conclusion: The clumpy structures observed in high-redshift galaxies reflect a highly compressible, shock-dominated ISM shaped by stellar feedback, and galaxy clumpiness could provide a complementary probe of bursty star formation in the early Universe. Observed samples may be biased towards galaxies caught in phases of elevated star formation.

title: Low Ly$α$ Visibility in Galaxy Overdensities: Reionization Topology and Neutral-Fraction Ceilings from DIVER over $4.8<z<11$
comment: 30 pages, 17 figures, 3 tables; submitted to ApJ
summary: Ly-alpha emission is widely used to trace cosmic reionization, but its interpretation depends on how Ly-alpha visibility varies with galaxy environment. We use deep JWST/NIRSpec observations from Deep Insights into UV Spectroscopy at the Epoch of Reionization (DIVER) in GOODS-N to measure Ly-alpha visibility for 250 galaxies at 4.8<z<11. The sample contains 84 Ly-alpha detections, including 44 strong emitters with rest-frame Ly-alpha equivalent width W_Lyalpha>25 A. We combine these measurements with H-alpha and [O III] emitters from JWST/NIRCam wide-field slitless spectroscopy to map the density field around each DIVER galaxy. Galaxies with high Ly-alpha equivalent widths (W_Lyalpha>25 A) or high effective Ly-alpha escape fractions (f_esc,Lyalpha^eff>0.05) tend to lie farther from nearby H-alpha and [O III] emitters than galaxies with lower Ly-alpha visibility. The clearest signal occurs near the prominent GOODS-N overdensity at z~5.2, where fewer than 15% of galaxies show strong Ly-alpha emission. This trend is opposite to the simplest inside-out reionization expectation that overdensities produce larger ionized regions and enhance Ly-alpha visibility. Possible explanations include circumgalactic and local intergalactic opacity, dense absorbers, and gas kinematics. We also derive an empirical upper envelope for f_esc,Lyalpha^eff and calibrate it with reionization simulations. Interpreting this envelope as a limiting IGM-attenuation signal gives neutral-fraction ceilings of <x_HI>_max=0.36, 0.76, 0.74, 0.84, and 1.0 at z~5.2, 5.8, 6.7, 7.7, and 9.8, respectively. The z~8 ceiling disfavors an almost completely neutral IGM at this epoch. These results support patchy reionization already underway by z~8 and show that galaxy Ly-alpha visibility encodes both large-scale ionization topology and near-source gas structure.

AI.tldr: Using JWST/NIRSpec observations from the DIVER survey, this paper measures Ly-alpha visibility for 250 galaxies at 4.8<z<11 and finds that strong Ly-alpha emitters tend to lie in lower-density environments, opposite to the simplest inside-out reionization expectation. The data constrain neutral fraction ceilings and support patchy reionization by z~8.
AI.motivation: Ly-alpha emission is a key tracer of cosmic reionization, but its interpretation depends on understanding how Ly-alpha visibility varies with galaxy environment. Previous studies have been limited by small samples or lacked environmental density information, making it difficult to distinguish between large-scale ionization topology effects and local gas structures.
AI.method: The authors use deep JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy from the DIVER survey in GOODS-N to measure Ly-alpha visibility for 250 galaxies at 4.8<z<11, containing 84 Ly-alpha detections (44 with W_Lyalpha>25 A). They combine these measurements with H-alpha and [O III] emitters from JWST/NIRCam wide-field slitless spectroscopy to map the density field around each galaxy and correlate Ly-alpha visibility with environment.
AI.result: Galaxies with high Ly-alpha equivalent widths or effective escape fractions tend to lie farther from nearby H-alpha and [O III] emitters. The clearest signal is near the GOODS-N overdensity at z~5.2, where fewer than 15% of galaxies show strong Ly-alpha emission. This is opposite to inside-out reionization expectations. They derive neutral-fraction ceilings of <x_HI>_max=0.36, 0.76, 0.74, 0.84, and 1.0 at z~5.2, 5.8, 6.7, 7.7, and 9.8 respectively, with the z~8 ceiling disfavoring an almost completely neutral IGM.
AI.conclusion: The results support patchy reionization already underway by z~8 and demonstrate that galaxy Ly-alpha visibility encodes both large-scale ionization topology and near-source gas structure. The anti-correlation between Ly-alpha visibility and environmental density challenges the simplest inside-out reionization scenario, suggesting contributions from circumgalactic opacity, dense absorbers, and gas kinematics.

title: Detectable subhalo impacts in Milky Way streams
summary: Dark matter subhalos leave gravitational imprints in the stellar streams of the Milky Way. Observing individual strong impacts of subhalos offers a compelling way to constrain and discover potentially dark subhalos down to $10^6 M_\odot$, allowing for new tests of the particle physics properties of dark matter. We develop a pipeline and statistical framework to forecast the expected number of detectable subhalo impacts on stellar streams, based on morphological and kinematic data from surveys such as LSST and Via. Starting from a catalog of confirmed stellar streams, we focus our efforts on 14 promising streams that are relatively well-modeled with a particle spray algorithm. Our criteria for a detectable impact is a deviation at 95% CL from the best-fit polynomial proxy model for the stream, which accounts for stream modeling uncertainties and regulates the effect of distant impacts that are degenerate with these uncertainties. Among the 14 streams studied, we find that 5 streams have an expected number of detectable impacts greater than 0.2. With LSST and Via data, the stream Jet has $5.15^{+1.10}_{-0.95}$ expected detectable impacts, followed by Orphan-Chenab ($1.40^{+0.62}_{-0.47}$), ATLAS-Aliqa Uma ($1.25^{+0.60}_{-0.44}$), GD-1 ($0.55^{+0.43}_{-0.28}$), and Palomar 5 ($0.40^{+0.39}_{-0.23}$), where error bars are the 95% containment on the Poisson mean. These values rely on the assumed subhalo population, which can give a factor of few systematic uncertainty in the predictions. We also consider effects of different particle dark matter models on the number of impacts, finding a suppression by a factor of $\sim 4$ for warm dark matter and fuzzy dark matter models at their current mass bounds and an $O(1)$ enhancement for a toy model of self-interacting dark matter.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a pipeline and statistical framework to forecast the number of detectable dark matter subhalo impacts on Milky Way stellar streams using LSST and Via survey data. Among 14 promising streams studied, 5 are expected to have detectable impacts, with stream Jet having the highest expectation of 5.15 detectable impacts. The framework also evaluates how different particle dark matter models (warm, fuzzy, self-interacting) affect these predictions.
AI.motivation: Dark matter subhalos leave gravitational imprints on stellar streams, and detecting individual strong impacts offers a powerful way to discover and constrain dark subhalos down to ~10^6 solar masses, enabling new tests of dark matter particle physics properties.
AI.method: The authors develop a forecasting pipeline using a particle spray algorithm to model 14 confirmed stellar streams. Detectability is based on a 95% CL deviation from a best-fit polynomial proxy model that accounts for stream modeling uncertainties. They compute expected Poisson means for detectable subhalo impacts and assess systematic uncertainties from the assumed subhalo population and different dark matter models.
AI.result: Five streams have expected detectable impacts > 0.2: Jet (5.15), Orphan-Chenab (1.40), ATLAS-Aliqa Uma (1.25), GD-1 (0.55), and Palomar 5 (0.40). Warm and fuzzy dark matter suppress impacts by ~4x at current mass bounds, while self-interacting dark matter gives an O(1) enhancement. Subhalo population assumptions introduce a factor of few systematic uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides concrete forecasts for detectable subhalo impacts on stellar streams, identifying the most promising streams for future detection efforts and demonstrating that stream impact observations can discriminate between different particle dark matter models.

title: Serendipitous discovery of an almost-dark galaxy in the Virgo Cluster
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A Letters
summary: Analogues of extreme Local Group galaxies with very low surface brightness and large effective radii must exist elsewhere, still hidden due to current detection limits. We report the serendipitous discovery of a low-mass almost-dark galaxy TTT J1237327+143535 in the Virgo Cluster, observed using the Two-meter Twin Telescope at the Teide Observatory. TTT J1237327+143535 has a central surface brightness of $27.9 \pm 0.2 \, \mathrm{mag arcsec}^{-2}$ in the $g'$-band, an effective radius of $0.9 \pm 0.1 \, \mathrm{kpc}$, and a total stellar mass of $(2.2 \pm 0.4) \times 10^6 \, \mathrm{M_\odot}$. Its effective radius and absolute magnitude are similar to those of galaxies And XXI and And XXIII. The discovery of this extremely low surface brightness, extended, low-mass galaxy suggests the existence of a significant population of almost-dark galaxies in the Virgo Cluster. An in-depth analysis of the Next Generation Virgo Cluster survey, as well as upcoming Rubin Data Releases and the 10-year Rubin Legacy Survey of Space and Time are expected to reveal large samples of this extreme galaxy population, which offers insights on galaxy formation in extreme conditions.

AI.tldr: A serendipitous discovery of an almost-dark, extremely low surface brightness dwarf galaxy (TTT J1237327+143535) in the Virgo Cluster, with properties similar to Local Group ultra-faint galaxies And XXI and And XXIII, suggesting a significant hidden population of such galaxies detectable by upcoming Rubin Observatory surveys.
AI.motivation: Analogues of extreme Local Group galaxies with very low surface brightness and large effective radii must exist elsewhere but remain hidden due to current detection limits, warranting the search for such extreme galaxy populations.
AI.method: Serendipitous discovery using the Two-meter Twin Telescope at the Teide Observatory; measured central surface brightness in the g'-band, effective radius, and total stellar mass; comparison of properties with Local Group galaxies And XXI and And XXIII.
AI.result: TTT J1237327+143535 has central surface brightness of 27.9 ± 0.2 mag arcsec^-2 in g'-band, effective radius of 0.9 ± 0.1 kpc, and stellar mass of (2.2 ± 0.4) × 10^6 M_sun; its effective radius and absolute magnitude are similar to And XXI and And XXIII.
AI.conclusion: The discovery implies a significant population of almost-dark galaxies in the Virgo Cluster; future NGVS analysis, Rubin Data Releases, and the 10-year Rubin LSST are expected to uncover large samples of this extreme population, providing insights into galaxy formation in extreme conditions.

title: The intrinsic luminosity-decay correlation in subsamples of GRB X-ray afterglows
comment: 21 pages, 24 figures, accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: The intrinsic luminosity-decay correlation in gamma-ray burst (GRB) afterglows, between the early-time luminosity and the average rate of decay past this time, has previously been observed in the radio, optical/UV, X-ray and GeV wavebands and quantitatively shows that more luminous afterglows tend to have higher average rates of decay. We have compiled an updated sample of 427 X-ray afterglows with measured redshifts, observed with Swift/XRT over 20 years. For each GRB, we measure the luminosity at 200 seconds in the rest frame, $L_{\mathrm{X,200s}}$, and the average rate of decay from this time, $α_{X,>200s}$. We find these parameters are correlated with a Spearman's rank coefficient ($R_\mathrm{sp}$) of $0.54\pm0.04$ at a significance of $\geq3σ$ and a linear regression slope of $0.18\pm0.02$. We separate our sample into subsamples, including 395 long GRBs (LGRBs) and 32 short GRBs (SGRBs) and find evidence of the $L_{\mathrm{X,200s}}$-$α_{X,>200s}$ correlation at a significance of $\geq3σ$ in LGRBs but not in SGRBs, consistent with previous studies. In a subsample of 102 LGRBs with well-sampled light curves and late end times, we find that scatter in the correlation is significantly reduced and the strength increases to $R_\mathrm{sp}=0.80\pm0.04$ whilst the slope remains consistent with the full sample. We discuss our results and, briefly, their potential implications on constraining the cause of the correlation. Possible causes include geometric effects due to the angle between the observer and the jet-axis, or some mechanism that regulates the rate at which energy is released by the GRB central engine.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the luminosity-decay correlation in GRB X-ray afterglows using a sample of 427 Swift/XRT afterglows with measured redshifts over 20 years. The correlation between luminosity at 200s and average decay rate is confirmed with R_sp=0.54±0.04, exists in long GRBs but not short GRBs, and strengthens to R_sp=0.80±0.04 in a well-sampled subsample of 102 LGRBs.
AI.motivation: The intrinsic luminosity-decay correlation in GRB afterglows has been observed across multiple wavebands, showing that more luminous afterglows decay faster. This study aims to confirm and quantify this correlation using an updated, larger X-ray sample and explore potential causes including geometric jet-angle effects or central engine energy-release mechanisms.
AI.method: The authors compiled 427 X-ray afterglows observed with Swift/XRT over 20 years, measured the luminosity at 200 seconds in the rest frame (L_X,200s) and the average decay rate after this time (α_X,>200s) for each GRB. They performed Spearman's rank correlation and linear regression analysis on the full sample, then separated into long and short GRB subsamples, and further examined a well-sampled subsample of 102 LGRBs.
AI.result: The full sample shows a correlation with Spearman's rank coefficient R_sp=0.54±0.04 at ≥3σ significance and a linear regression slope of 0.18±0.02. The correlation exists in 395 LGRBs but not in 32 SGRBs. For 102 well-sampled LGRBs, the correlation strengthens to R_sp=0.80±0.04 with reduced scatter while the slope remains consistent.
AI.conclusion: The luminosity-decay correlation in X-ray afterglows is robustly confirmed in the full and long GRB samples but absent in short GRBs. The stronger correlation in well-sampled LGRBs suggests improved light-curve quality reveals the underlying relation more clearly. Possible physical causes include geometric effects from the observer-to-jet-axis angle or mechanisms regulating central engine energy release.

title: Reconstructing orbits of galaxies in extreme regions (roger v2.0): an extension to intermediate mass systems
comment: Code hosted at https://github.com/Martindelosrios/pyROGER. Prepared for submission to MNRAS
summary: In this paper, we present an updated version of the roger code, called roger v2.0, developed to perform the orbital classification of galaxies residing in and around galaxy groups and clusters. In addition to the projected phase-space coordinates, the new version incorporates the host halo mass as an additional input parameter. Although the inclusion of the halo mass leads to only modest changes in the classification, it contributes to improving the overall robustness of the method. We also extend the range of host halo masses over which roger can be applied, enabling the analysis of systems with masses down to $10^{13.5} h^{-1} M_{\odot}$. We further provide a Python implementation of the new code, which will be made publicly available. This implementation enables users to efficiently and robustly classify arbitrary galaxy samples using either version of the method. Moreover, it allows users to train a customized classifier on an alternative training set, providing the flexibility to adapt the method to different datasets and scientific applications.

AI.tldr: roger v2.0 is an updated code for orbital classification of galaxies in and around groups and clusters, now incorporating host halo mass as an additional input, extending applicability to lower-mass systems (~10^13.5 h^-1 M_sun), and providing a public Python implementation with customizable training capabilities.
AI.motivation: To improve the robustness and applicability of the roger orbital classification code by incorporating host halo mass as an additional input parameter, extending its range to lower-mass halos, and providing a flexible, publicly available Python implementation.
AI.method: The updated roger v2.0 method adds host halo mass as a third input parameter alongside projected phase-space coordinates (projected distance and line-of-sight velocity). A Python implementation is provided that supports both the original and updated versions, and allows users to train custom classifiers on alternative training datasets.
AI.result: Including host halo mass yields modest but notable improvements in classification robustness. The method now supports host halo masses down to 10^13.5 h^-1 M_sun, broadening its range of applicability compared to the previous version.
AI.conclusion: roger v2.0 offers an enhanced, publicly accessible Python tool for orbital classification of galaxies, with increased robustness and flexibility, applicable to a wider range of halo masses and adaptable to various datasets and scientific needs.

title: Modeling Relativistic Tidal Disruptions of MESA Stars
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures
summary: Tidal disruption events (TDEs) occur when a star passes so close to a black hole that its self-gravity is overcome by the external tidal field. As the star passes, it initially deforms, then is ripped apart, and some of its material eventually falls back on bound orbits, forming an accretion disk around the black hole. A Newtonian model of TDEs, based on stellar perturbation theory of MESA stars, was recently introduced as an alternative to computationally intensive hydrodynamical simulations. In this work, we add relativistic corrections to the model, incorporating equatorial Kerr geodesics, relativistic tidal fields, and relativistic fallback times. Compared to the Newtonian case, we find that stars are disrupted earlier in their orbit, which gives them less time to accumulate physical deformations. Additionally, we find that the increased distance from the black hole at the time of disruption makes the fallback time longer. However, the black hole spin has a negligible impact on fallback time, except for orbits with exceptionally close pericenter. Our results allow for a more accurate calculation of fallback rates than the Newtonian model, while also remaining computationally cheap. The code is available on GitHub.

AI.tldr: This paper extends a previously developed Newtonian tidal disruption event (TDE) model—based on stellar perturbation theory of MESA stars—by incorporating relativistic corrections, including Kerr geodesics, relativistic tidal fields, and relativistic fallback times, enabling more accurate fallback-rate calculations at low computational cost.
AI.motivation: TDEs are computationally expensive to study via hydrodynamical simulations. A Newtonian perturbation-theory-based model exists as a cheaper alternative, but it lacks relativistic physics that are important near black holes. Adding relativistic corrections improves accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency.
AI.method: The authors augment the Newtonian TDE model with general relativistic effects by incorporating equatorial Kerr geodesics for stellar trajectories, relativistic tidal fields for deformation calculations, and relativistic expressions for fallback times, all applied to MESA-generated stellar models.
AI.result: In the relativistic model, stars are disrupted earlier in their orbit, leaving less time for physical deformation to accumulate. The greater distance from the black hole at disruption leads to longer fallback times. Black hole spin has negligible effect on fallback time except for very close pericenter orbits.
AI.conclusion: The relativistic model provides more accurate fallback-rate predictions than the Newtonian counterpart while remaining computationally cheap. The code is publicly available on GitHub.

title: Tracing Lyman alpha escape in the CRISTAL-02 galaxy at z~5.3
comment: 13 pages, 8 figures, 1 table. Accepted for publication in A&A
summary:
Aim. We investigate the mechanisms regulating Lyman-alpha (Ly-a) escape in the star-forming galaxy CRISTAL-02 at z~5.3. The galaxy hosts five distinct clumps, with Clumps A and B suggested as potential active galactic nuclei (AGN) candidates. We study how AGN or star formation activity influences the spatial distribution and escape of Ly-a emission.
  Methods. Using VLT/MUSE Ly-a and JWST/NIRSpec IFU H-a and H-b observations, complemented by NIRCam UV imaging, we constructed spatially matched emission-line maps. We derived flux, line-ratio, and extinction maps, together with spatially resolved Ly-a escape fractions and ionizing photon production efficiencies.
  Results. Ly-a emission extends preferentially along the [C ii] outflow direction, while H-a and UV trace the galactic disk. Clumps A and B show contrasting properties: Clump A, with lower dust attenuation, exhibits enhanced Ly-a/H-a ratios and a higher Ly-a escape fraction, whereas Clump B shows stronger H-a and UV emission but suppressed Ly-a. These results suggest that Ly-a escape is influenced by outflows, dust attenuation, and local gas conditions.
  Conclusions. We present spatially resolved measurements of the Ly-a escape fraction and ionizing photon production efficiency in a galaxy at z~5.3, highlighting the role of feedback-driven gas clearing and anisotropic outflows in shaping Ly-a emission. The evidence favors an outflow, but the available data cannot uniquely distinguish between AGN- and star formation-driven feedback. Future spatially resolved Ly-a, H-a, and [C ii] observations will be crucial for identifying the dominant feedback mechanism.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the mechanisms regulating Lyman-alpha escape in the z~5.3 star-forming galaxy CRISTAL-02, using spatially resolved VLT/MUSE Ly-a, JWST/NIRSpec IFU H-a and H-b observations. The study finds that Ly-a emission extends along outflow directions while H-a and UV trace the galactic disk, with clump-specific properties revealing that dust attenuation, outflows, and local gas conditions—not uniquely AGN or star formation—shape Ly-a escape.
AI.motivation: To understand what regulates the escape of Lyman-alpha emission in high-redshift galaxies, particularly whether AGN or star formation activity drives the spatial distribution and escape of Ly-a photons in CRISTAL-02, a galaxy hosting potential AGN candidates.
AI.method: Combined VLT/MUSE Ly-a and JWST/NIRSpec IFU H-a and H-b observations with NIRCam UV imaging to construct spatially matched emission-line maps. Derived flux, line-ratio, extinction maps, along with spatially resolved Ly-a escape fractions and ionizing photon production efficiencies.
AI.result: Ly-a emission extends preferentially along the [C ii] outflow direction while H-a and UV trace the galactic disk. Clump A (lower dust attenuation) shows enhanced Ly-a/H-a ratios and higher escape fractions, whereas Clump B shows stronger H-a and UV emission but suppressed Ly-a. Evidence favors an outflow but cannot uniquely distinguish AGN- versus star formation-driven feedback.
AI.conclusion: Presents spatially resolved Ly-a escape fraction and ionizing photon production efficiency measurements at z~5.3, highlighting the roles of feedback-driven gas clearing and anisotropic outflows in shaping Ly-a emission. Future spatially resolved Ly-a, H-a, and [C ii] observations are needed to identify the dominant feedback mechanism.

title: Outflows in steep density gradients: diversity of behavior and implications for tidal disruption events and luminous fast blue optical transients
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures
summary: Powerful explosions may undergo sustained energy injection as a central engine launches a wind into the surrounding gas, generating a forward and a reverse shock separated by a contact discontinuity. During the adiabatic phase, the dynamics depend strongly on the wind-to-ambient density ratio $f \equiv ρ_{\rm w} / ρ_{\rm a}$. For $f << 1$, the reverse shock lies well inside the contact discontinuity, and the mechanical energy deposited by the wind is retained in a radially extended, approximately isobaric shocked-wind region whose pressure drives the swept-up ambient shell. For $f \gg 1$, the reverse shock remains close to the contact, and the expansion is governed by the ram-pressure interaction between the freely expanding wind and the swept-up ambient gas. We use analytic scalings and one-dimensional shock-capturing hydrodynamic simulations to determine how outflows in these two limits evolve in ambient density profiles $ρ_{\rm a} \propto r^{-n}$, where $2 \leq n \leq 3$, and whether their shock structures accelerate or coast at constant velocity. For $n > 2$, initially underdense outflows produce accelerating forward shocks whose radii evolve as $R_{\rm s} \propto t^{3/(5-n)}$. Because $ρ_{\rm w} \propto r^{-2}$, f increases with radius, causing the reverse-shocked wind region to contract relative to the contact position as the forward shock transitions toward constant-velocity expansion. This occurs when $f \sim$ a few at $t_{\rm dec} \propto f_0^{1/(2-n)}$, where $f_0$ is the initial wind-to-ambient density ratio. By contrast, outflows initialized with $f_0 \gg 1$ do not develop an extended accelerating phase and remain approximately coasting throughout their adiabatic evolution. We discuss applications to tidal disruption event outflows and luminous fast blue optical transients, whose environments are often inferred to have steep density profiles with $n > 2$.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the adiabatic dynamics of wind-driven explosions in power-law ambient density profiles, distinguishing two regimes based on the wind-to-ambient density ratio f. For f << 1, a radially extended isobaric shocked-wind region drives the swept-up shell; for f >> 1, ram-pressure interaction dominates. Using analytic scalings and 1D hydrodynamic simulations, the authors show that in steep profiles (n > 2), underdense outflows develop accelerating forward shocks (R_s ∝ t^{3/(5-n)}) that later transition to coasting as f increases, while initially overdense outflows coast throughout. Applications to TDEs and LFBOTs are discussed.
AI.motivation: To understand how sustained energy injection from a central engine wind affects the dynamics of explosive outflows, particularly the evolution of their forward and reverse shock structures in power-law ambient density profiles with n > 2, which are relevant to astrophysical transients like tidal disruption events and luminous fast blue optical transients.
AI.method: The authors employ analytic scaling arguments combined with one-dimensional shock-capturing hydrodynamic simulations. They examine two asymptotic regimes of wind-to-ambient density ratio f (underdense f << 1 and overdense f >> 1) and track the evolution of shock structures in ambient density profiles ρ_a ∝ r^{-n} for 2 ≤ n ≤ 3, monitoring whether shocks accelerate or coast.
AI.result: For n > 2, underdense outflows (f << 1) produce accelerating forward shocks with R_s ∝ t^{3/(5-n)}. Since ρ_w ∝ r^{-2}, f increases with radius, causing the reverse-shocked wind region to contract relative to the contact discontinuity, and the forward shock transitions to constant-velocity expansion when f ~ few at t_dec ∝ f_0^{1/(2-n)}. Outflows with f_0 >> 1 do not experience an extended accelerating phase and coast throughout their adiabatic evolution.
AI.conclusion: The dynamics of wind-driven explosions depend sensitively on the initial wind-to-ambient density ratio and the ambient density slope. Underdense winds in steep profiles (n > 2) initially accelerate but eventually transition to coasting when the wind compression catches up. Overdense winds remain coasting throughout. These results are relevant for interpreting TDE outflows and LFBOTs, whose environments often have n > 2.

title: The VariableTNG project: mass-dependent regulation of galaxy morphology by baryonic feedback
summary: Galaxy morphology is shaped by both assembly history and baryonic processes, but their relative roles remain uncertain. We use the VariableTNG (VTNG) simulation suite to investigate how variations in baryonic feedback regulate galaxy morphology while keeping the initial conditions fixed. VTNG consists of cosmological magnetohydrodynamic simulations performed with the moving-mesh code {\sc AREPO}, varying eight parameters governing stellar and AGN feedback. At $z=1$, we characterize morphology using $κ_{\rm co}$, $v/σ$, and the axis ratio $c/a$. We find substantial morphological diversity across feedback models, with the dominant mechanism strongly dependent on stellar mass. For $M_\ast \lesssim 10^{11}\,{\rm M_\odot}$, morphology is primarily controlled by the supernova temperature $T_{\rm SN}$: larger $T_{\rm SN}$ delays early star formation, promotes a denser and more rotationally supported gas reservoir, and favours subsequent disc growth through in-situ star formation. At higher masses, morphology becomes increasingly sensitive to AGN feedback, particularly the quasar-mode coupling efficiency $ε_{\rm f,high}$. Higher $ε_{\rm f,high}$ suppresses early black hole growth, thereby weakening subsequent radio-mode feedback associated with gas depletion and loss of rotational support. The resulting morphology--mass relation is non-monotonic, with maximum rotational support at intermediate stellar masses. Our results demonstrate that baryonic feedback regulates galaxy morphology through distinct mass-dependent pathways, with stellar feedback dominating at lower masses and AGN self-regulation becoming increasingly important at the massive end.

AI.tldr: Using the VariableTNG simulation suite, this paper shows that baryonic feedback regulates galaxy morphology through mass-dependent pathways: supernova temperature controls morphology at lower stellar masses (≲10^11 M⊙) by delaying early star formation and promoting disc growth, while AGN feedback (especially quasar-mode coupling efficiency) dominates at higher masses by suppressing early black hole growth and preserving rotational support. The resulting morphology-mass relation is non-monotonic with maximum rotational support at intermediate masses.
AI.motivation: Galaxy morphology is shaped by both assembly history and baryonic processes, but their relative roles remain uncertain. The authors aim to disentangle these contributions by systematically varying baryonic feedback parameters while keeping initial conditions fixed.
AI.method: The authors use the VariableTNG (VTNG) simulation suite, consisting of cosmological magnetohydrodynamic simulations with the moving-mesh code AREPO. They vary eight parameters governing stellar and AGN feedback while keeping initial conditions fixed. At z=1, morphology is characterized using three metrics: κ_co (kinematic parameter), v/σ (rotation-to-dispersion ratio), and axis ratio c/a.
AI.result: Substantial morphological diversity is found across feedback models. For M_* ≲ 10^11 M⊙, morphology is primarily controlled by supernova temperature T_SN, where larger values delay early star formation, promote denser rotationally supported gas, and favor disc growth via in-situ star formation. At higher masses, morphology becomes sensitive to AGN feedback, particularly quasar-mode coupling efficiency ε_f,high, where higher values suppress early black hole growth and weaken radio-mode feedback. The morphology-mass relation is non-monotonic with maximum rotational support at intermediate stellar masses.
AI.conclusion: Baryonic feedback regulates galaxy morphology through distinct mass-dependent pathways: stellar feedback dominates at lower masses while AGN self-regulation becomes increasingly important at the massive end.

title: Discovery of Three Glitches in the previously quiet pulsar PSR J1637$-$4642
comment: 13 pages, 7 figures, 3 tables, accepted for publication in ApJ (2026)
summary: We present the discovery and analysis of three rotational glitches in the young pulsar PSR J1637$-$4642. title: The UKIRT M33 Monitoring Project: A 15-Year Near-Infrared Variable Star Catalogue for the Central Kiloparsec, and Prospects for Star Formation History and Dust Return

title: First Observational Evidence for QPO-like Coevolution between Characteristic Damping Timescales and X-ray Time Lags among AGNs
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables
summary: Quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) and stochastic variability provide complementary probes of the inner accretion flow around supermassive black holes in active galactic nuclei (AGNs). Previous multi-epoch studies of narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxy RE~J1034+396 revealed a coevolution between the QPO frequency and the X-ray time lag, but whether the stochastic variability participates in the same structural evolution has remained unclear. We obtain reliable characteristic damping timescales (CDTs) for 17 observations, with the soft-band CDT consistently longer than its hard-band counterpart. When combined with the X-ray time lag, the hard-band CDT traces a counterclockwise closed loop that closely resembles the previously reported QPO-frequency--time-lag loop, whereas the soft-band CDT exhibits more complex trajectory. Under plausible dynamical, thermal, and viscous interpretations, the hard-band CDT is associated with characteristic scales in the inner hot accretion flow/corona. The observed loops may represent different projections of a common cyclic evolution of the inner accretion flow/corona, as the three timing observables may respond to its dynamical, stochastic, and radiative properties on different timescales. These results provide the first observational support among AGNs for the physical picture in which changes in the spatial extent of the hot inner flow/corona simultaneously affect QPO and stochastic variability.

title: Diversity of Ionized Gas Structures in Nearby Metal-poor Dwarf Galaxies
comment: 15 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to PASJ. Comments are very welcome!
summary: We investigate whether optical and far-infrared [O III] emission from nearby metal-poor dwarf galaxies can be represented by a homogeneous one-zone ionized-gas model with a single electron temperature and density. Our sample comprises five galaxies from the Herschel Dwarf Galaxy Survey: HS1222+3741, SBS0335-052E, POX186, Haro11, and IZw18. We combine galaxy-integrated or nearly galaxy-integrated [O III] 4363 and 5007 measurements from Seimei/KOOLS-IFU observations and published or archival spectroscopy with Herschel/PACS [O III] 88um measurements. Because [O III] 4363 is not detected in HS1222+3741, the analysis is based on the remaining four galaxies. SBS0335-052E and Haro11 lie near or slightly beyond the low-density boundary of the one-zone diagnostic. Their nominal line ratios favor effective densities of ne<1cm-3, while conservative treatment of the uncertainties allows values up to 40 and 10cm-3, respectively. These remain substantially below densities inferred from independent diagnostics. By contrast, POX186 and IZw18 show no significant discrepancy between the optical--far-infrared [O III] and low-ionization optical diagnostics. Additional optical and ultraviolet diagnostics show that inferred densities can span several orders of magnitude within a galaxy. Representative two-zone models reproduce the [O III] 4363, 5007, and 88um emission in SBS0335-052E and Haro11 by combining relatively dense gas with cooler, low-density gas. The low-density component contributes approximately 61% and 72% of the 88um luminosity, but only 14% and 23% of the 5007 luminosity, respectively. These solutions are not unique and may represent a broader unresolved distribution of gas conditions. Our results show that temperatures and densities inferred from integrated one-zone analyses are effective quantities and that similar diagnostic discrepancies can arise in nearby metal-poor galaxies.

AI.motivation: To assess whether the common practice of using a single homogeneous one-zone ionized-gas model to interpret integrated [O III] emission (optical + far-infrared) is valid for nearby metal-poor dwarf galaxies, where multiphase gas structures may bias inferred physical conditions.

title: Multi-scale Memory and Regime Shift in the Hyperactive Repeating FRB 20240114A
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures, 1 table. Comments are welcome!
summary: We present a statistical analysis of FRB~20240114A, a hyperactive repeating fast radio burst, based on 11,553 bursts detected by FAST over 214 days. Our main findings are fourfold. (1) On the most active day (MJD~60381, 3,197 bursts in 4.38 hr), event-rate coherence analysis reveals persistent correlated activity extending up to 3600~s, the longest reported for any repeating FRB, showing memory persists even in intense bursting epochs. (2) The waiting-time distribution on this day is well described by three exponentials, whereas the full 214-day sample develops a threshold power-law tail, indicating burst statistics depend on the observational baseline, with long-range correlations emerging only over longer timescales, a hallmark of self-organized criticality. (3) Rescaled range (R/S) analysis of waiting times reveals a broken power law, with Hurst exponents $H_1=0.63\pm0.02$ (short-lag weak memory) and $H_2=1.04\pm0.02$ (long-lag non-stationary drift). The break corresponds to $\sim$1 hour, consistent with the 3600~s coherence limit. R/S analysis of energies similarly exhibits a break ($H_1=0.60\pm0.01$, $H_2=1.10\pm0.05$) at a different lag, reinforcing that non-stationarity affects both temporal and energetic properties. (4) Energy distributions exhibit waiting-time-dependent slopes that are consistent with the full and daily samples, and the high-energy cutoff remains constant across waiting-time groups, suggesting that the maximum energy scale is an intrinsic source property. Together, these results establish a multi-scale memory framework: the source behaves stochastically on short timescales but exhibits systemic non-stationarity over months, providing benchmarks for burst models and highlighting the need for long-term, high-cadence monitoring to capture temporal complexity.

AI.method: Statistical analysis of 11,553 bursts from FAST observations over 214 days, employing: event-rate coherence analysis; waiting-time distribution fitting (exponential versus power-law models); rescaled range (R/S) analysis to compute Hurst exponents for both waiting times and energies; and energy distribution analysis partitioned by waiting-time groups.

The results support self-organized criticality with long-range correlations emerging only over longer observational baselines, and emphasize the need for long-term, high-cadence monitoring to fully capture temporal complexity in repeating FRBs.

title: OutThere Survey: Addressing $\mathrm{ξ_{ion}}$ and $\mathrm{f_{esc}}$ with a population of average galaxies at z$\sim$2
comment: 20 pages, 13 figures, 5 tables
summary: Constraining the major contributors to the ionisation of the early universe is an ongoing endeavour of high-redshift galaxy research. We measure the ionising photon production efficiency and Lyman Continuum escape fraction for a sample of 230 intermediate redshift ($1.3<z<2.6$) sources observed as a part of the \textit{OutThere survey}; a pure-parallel, wide-area JWST/NIRISS survey with accompanying JWST/NIRCam, NIRISS and HST photometry. The low threshold emission selection criteria for this sample makes for a large and robust control, against which other works may be contrasted, particularly for low-mass galaxies above z$>$5. This control sample allows us to verify the correlations between ionising and spectral/physical properties suggested by previous studies. We find no significant correlations between the ionising photon production efficiency ($\mathrm{ξ_{ion}}$) with the UV slope, $\mathrm{M_{UV}}$, M$_*$ or sSFR. We do find that $\mathrm{ξ_{ion}}$ correlates with [OIII]5007Å\, equivalent width (EW) (Spearman coefficient $ρ$ =0.24; p$< 4\times10^{-4}$) and H$α$ EW ($ρ$ =0.63; p$<< 1\times10^{-6}$) hold even at low EW albeit with more scatter. We also find that our novel approach to determining the ionising photon escape fraction $\mathrm{f_{esc}}$ results in values within theoretical ranges (0-10\%) though vary substantially in comparison to the empirical results (median $\mathrm{f_{esc}} = 0.9\%^{+1.1}_{-0.5}$ including non-detections, median $\mathrm{f_{esc}} = 1.9\%^{+8.9}_{-1.8}$ above a $0.01\%$ threshold). We find that this escape fraction method has consistently significant correlations with the redshift, SFR and M$_{UV}$ and sample-dependent correlations with [OIII]5007Å\,EW,H$α$ EW and stellar mass.

AI.method: Using the OutThere survey—a pure-parallel, wide-area JWST/NIRISS survey with JWST/NIRCam, NIRISS and HST photometry—they measure ξ_ion and f_esc for 230 intermediate-redshift sources (1.3<z<2.6) using low threshold emission selection. title: Quasi-periodic Eruptions from Recurrent Satellite Black Hole Transits through Magnetized Galactic Nucleus Accretion Disks
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure
summary: Quasi-periodic eruptions (QPEs) are recurrent soft X-ray flares from galactic nuclei, but their origin remains uncertain. The delayed ultraviolet (UV) counterpart detected in Ansky provides a new constraint on viable models. We present a two-channel model in which a satellite black hole (sBH) repeatedly crosses a nuclear accretion disk threaded by a large-scale magnetic field. Gravitational focusing and dynamical drag generate hot, optically thick ejecta whose expansion and photon diffusion power the soft X-ray QPE. For fiducial Bondi-scale parameters, the model yields a characteristic X-ray duration of $\sim10^3\ \mathrm{s}$ and luminosity of $\sim10^{42}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$; at lower orbital inclinations, the duration extends to the day-long scale observed in Ansky. Simultaneously, the sBH motion compresses and bends the background magnetic field, triggering in-disk reconnection. The dissipated energy then emerges after photon diffusion as a broader, delayed UV response. The resulting thermal power is comparable to the variable UV luminosity of Ansky. Unfavorable magnetic fields or diffusion times longer than the QPE recurrence period can weaken or smear out the UV signal, potentially explaining the lack of clear UV counterparts in other QPE sources.

The model simultaneously explains both the soft X-ray QPEs (from gravitational focusing and dynamical drag producing hot ejecta) and the delayed UV counterpart observed in Ansky (from magnetic field compression triggering reconnection and photon-diffusion-delayed thermal emission).

AI.method: The model uses a two-channel framework: (1) an X-ray channel where gravitational focusing and dynamical drag during sBH-disk crossings generate hot, optically thick ejecta whose expansion and photon diffusion produce soft X-ray QPEs; (2) a UV channel where the moving sBH compresses and bends the background magnetic field, triggering in-disk reconnection, with the dissipated energy emerging as a delayed UV response after photon diffusion.

The model also explains the absence of UV counterparts in other QPE sources via unfavorable magnetic fields or diffusion times exceeding the recurrence period.
AI.conclusion: The two-channel sBH-disk interaction model provides a unified explanation for both the X-ray QPEs and the delayed UV counterpart in Ansky, and offers a natural explanation for the diversity of UV signatures across QPE sources.

title: ALOHA IRDCs Molecular Line Follow-up: I. Gas properties and kinematics
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures, accepted for publication on A&A
summary: Infrared Dark Clouds are ideal sites for investigating the initial conditions of massive star and cluster formation. title: J0011+3443: a GPS compact symmetric object, gravitational lens, or dual AGN?
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: We present new multi-frequency VLBA observations of \object{J0011+3443} (TXS\,0008+344, $z=0.89$) at 2.3, 4.9, 8.5, and, for the first time, 23.6\,GHz. The source consists of two compact components A and B at a projected separation of $314\pm2$\,pc, plus a third feature C detected at 23.6\,GHz at $0.6$\,mas from A. Archival low-resolution radio measurements confirm an integrated gigahertz-peaked spectrum, with an observed-frame peak frequency of $ν_\mathrm{peak}=0.73\pm0.08$\,GHz and a peak flux density of $S_\mathrm{peak}=879\pm125$\,mJy. Comparison with nearly frequency-matched low-resolution measurements shows that the VLBA recovers $0.85\pm0.11$ of the 4.85\,GHz flux density and $0.50\pm0.06$ of the 8.46\,GHz flux density. The lower recovered fraction at 8.5\,GHz suggests that low-surface-brightness emission is resolved out or falls below the VLBA surface-brightness sensitivity. We therefore interpret the VLBA component spectra as spectra of the compact recovered emission only. The 23.6\,GHz morphology, the absence of a detected flat-spectrum core, the similar compact spectra of A and B, and the steep integrated GHz spectrum favor an interpretation of \object{J0011+3443} as a GPS-class compact symmetric object, possibly in a short-lived or relic phase, although a dual-AGN origin cannot be excluded without multi-epoch astrometry.

title: Re-evaluating the resolved mass-metallicity relation with a self-consistent metallicity calibration
comment: 13 pages, 9 figures, accepted by A&A. Comments are welcome
summary: Aims. The mass-metallicity relation (MZR) is essential for understanding the chemical evolution of galaxies. Whether the star formation rate (SFR) plays a role in setting the metallicity has long been debated. Using various metallicity calibrations can result in different conclusions for this fundamental yet unresolved issue. Methods. We apply a self-consistent metallicity calibration based on photoionization models to re-evaluate the resolved and integrated MZR. We utilize the integral field unit data from SDSS-IV/MaNGA, with $\sim 3.5\times10^6$ spaxels and $\sim$ 4550 galaxies. We compare our preferred metallicity calibration with several strong-line calibrations in the literature and direct method metallicity. We analyze the metallicity residual of MZR to evaluate the effects of SFR and apply the partial correlation coefficient to quantify the effects. Results. The metallicity calibration we used shows the best consistency with the direct method. We provide 3 equations for resolved MZR, and verify that local SFR does not show significant correlation with metallicity. Considering the integrated properties, (s)SFR do not present correlation with the metallicity residuals. The results suggest that an equilibrium of inflow and outflow is favored, and the mass-metallicity relation does not have a secondary dependence on SFR.

AI.tldr: This study re-evaluates the mass-metallicity relation (MZR) using a self-consistent photoionization-based metallicity calibration applied to ~3.5 million spaxels from ~4,550 MaNGA galaxies. The authors find that their calibration is most consistent with the direct method and that neither local nor integrated star formation rate shows a significant secondary correlation with metallicity, favoring an equilibrium of inflow and outflow in galaxy chemical evolution.
AI.motivation: The mass-metallicity relation is fundamental to understanding galaxy chemical evolution, but whether star formation rate plays a secondary role in setting metallicity has been long debated. Different metallicity calibrations can lead to contradictory conclusions on this unresolved issue.
AI.method: The authors apply a self-consistent metallicity calibration based on photoionization models to re-evaluate resolved and integrated MZR using SDSS-IV/MaNGA integral field unit data (~3.5 million spaxels, ~4,550 galaxies). They compare their calibration with several strong-line calibrations and direct method metallicities, analyze metallicity residuals of the MZR for SFR effects, and use partial correlation coefficients to quantify these effects.
AI.result: The preferred metallicity calibration shows the best consistency with the direct method. Three equations for the resolved MZR are provided. Local SFR shows no significant correlation with metallicity, and integrated (specific) SFR also shows no correlation with metallicity residuals.
AI.conclusion: The results support an equilibrium between inflow and outflow in galaxy chemical evolution, and indicate that the mass-metallicity relation does not have a secondary dependence on star formation rate.

title: Probabilistic kilonova prediction from gravitational wave inferred binary neutron star parameters
summary: Kilonovae provide a key electromagnetic window into binary neutron star mergers, revealing the properties of the merging system while probing r-process nucleosynthesis of the Universe. However, only a few kilonova candidates have been detected to date, with AT2017gfo being the only one associated with a gravitational wave event, GW170817. In this work, we present \textsc{Genova}, a probabilistic framework for predicting kilonova spectra and light curves directly from gravitational wave posterior samples of binary neutron star mergers. This method uses a conditional normalising flow to learn the distribution of rest-frame spectra conditioned on the source-frame component masses, tidal deformabilities, viewing angle and time since merger. Other kilonova model parameters, such as ejecta opacities, are marginalised over during training, so that their effects are propagated into the predicted spectra as predictive uncertainty. In the self-consistency test, the flow model reproduces the median light curves with residuals typically below $\sim 0.1$ mag, and the ratio of the predicted central 68\% interval widths remains predominantly between $0.8$ and $1.4$ over $\sim 0.4$--$8.0$ days. Comparisons with a physically distinct kilonova model show that the probabilistic prediction can remain informative beyond the model used for training. We apply \textsc{Genova} to GW170817/AT2017gfo using multi-band observations, including newly re-reduced $Y$-, $J$-, $K_s$-band photometry from the Visible and Infrared Survey Telescope for Astronomy, which we present in this work. The resulting predictive intervals broadly encompass the observations while capturing both gravitational wave posterior uncertainty and the variation induced by marginalised kilonova model parameters.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Genova, a probabilistic framework using conditional normalizing flows to predict kilonova spectra and light curves directly from gravitational wave posterior samples of binary neutron star mergers, applying it to GW170817/AT2017gfo with new infrared photometry.
AI.motivation: Kilonovae offer crucial electromagnetic insight into binary neutron star mergers and r-process nucleosynthesis, but only a few candidates have been detected, with AT2017gfo being the only one tied to a gravitational wave event. A probabilistic framework that bridges gravitational wave posteriors to kilonova predictions is needed.
AI.method: Genova uses a conditional normalizing flow to learn the distribution of rest-frame spectra conditioned on source-frame component masses, tidal deformabilities, viewing angle, and time since merger. Non-learned kilonova model parameters (e.g., ejecta opacities) are marginalized during training, propagating their effects as predictive uncertainty.
AI.result: In self-consistency tests, the model reproduces median light curves with residuals below ~0.1 mag and predicted central 68% interval width ratios predominantly between 0.8 and 1.4 over ~0.4-8.0 days. The model remains informative against a physically distinct kilonova model. Applied to GW170817/AT2017gfo, predictive intervals broadly encompass multi-band observations, including newly re-reduced Y-, J-, K_s-band VISTA photometry presented in this work.
AI.conclusion: Genova successfully propagates gravitational wave posterior uncertainty and marginalised kilonova model parameter variation into predictive spectra and light curves, providing a robust probabilistic tool for kilonova forecasting from neutron star merger gravitational wave signals.

title: The Nearby Star Formation and Supernova Histories Reconstructed from Young Star Clusters
comment: 27 pages, 9 figures. Submitted to ApJ. Comments are welcome. An interactive 3D version of Figures 2 and 3 is available at https://cswigg.github.io/cam_website/oviz_figures/oviz_supernovae.html
summary: We reconstruct the recent star formation and core-collapse supernova (ccSN) histories of the Solar Neighborhood from the past trajectories of young star clusters. Using a \textit{Gaia}-based cluster sample with newly derived ages, masses, and bulk 3D velocities, we integrate orbits backward in an assumed axisymmetric Galactic potential and combine the trajectories with IMF sampling and stellar lifetimes to infer ccSN times and locations over the past 50 Myr. The result is an all-sky, 3D, time-resolved map of nearby ccSN activity for comparison with high-resolution 3D views of the local interstellar medium. The 0--15 Myr map shows strong enhancements toward Orion, Vela, Sco--Cen, and Cepheus, many within present-day cavities and shells. At earlier times, the dominant enhancements trace the Collinder 135, Messier 6, and Alpha Persei cluster families, showing how the remnants of massive star-forming complexes have shaped the recent local feedback history. We recover a bursty star formation history followed by a delayed, smoother ccSN history. Over the last 40 Myr, the mean star formation and ccSN rates are \(823~M_\odot~\mathrm{Myr}^{-1}\) and \(7.7~\mathrm{Myr}^{-1}\), respectively, corresponding to a Milky Way rate of \(0.55\pm0.03~\mathrm{century}^{-1}\). Present-day OB-star catalogs yield rates ranging from agreement with the cluster reconstruction to several times higher. Because the catalogs overlap weakly and require different corrections, we do not rescale the ccSN map. Our reconstruction provides an empirical framework for connecting the recent history of massive-star feedback to the 3D structure and life cycle of gas in the nearby Milky Way.

AI.tldr: The authors reconstruct the star formation and core-collapse supernova history of the Solar Neighborhood over the past 50 Myr by tracing young star clusters backward in time using Gaia-based cluster data, IMF sampling, and stellar lifetimes, producing a 3D time-resolved map of ccSN activity that shows enhancements toward Orion, Vela, Sco-Cen, and Cepheus, with mean rates of 823 Msun/Myr and 7.7 ccSN/Myr.
AI.motivation: To connect recent massive-star feedback to the observed 3D structure of the local interstellar medium by empirically reconstructing when and where core-collapse supernovae occurred in the Solar Neighborhood.
AI.method: Uses a Gaia-based young star cluster sample with newly derived ages, masses, and 3D velocities; integrates cluster orbits backward in an assumed axisymmetric Galactic potential; combines trajectories with IMF sampling and stellar lifetimes to infer ccSN times and locations over the past 50 Myr.
AI.result: Produces an all-sky 3D time-resolved ccSN map. The 0-15 Myr map shows strong enhancements toward Orion, Vela, Sco-Cen, and Cepheus, many within present-day cavities/shells. Earlier periods are dominated by Collinder 135, Messier 6, and Alpha Persei cluster families. The star formation history is bursty while the ccSN history is more smoothed/delayed. Mean rates over 40 Myr are 823 Msun/Myr (SFR) and 7.7/Myr (ccSN), corresponding to a Milky Way rate of 0.55±0.03 per century.
AI.conclusion: The reconstruction provides an empirical framework connecting recent massive-star feedback history to the 3D structure and life cycle of gas in the nearby Milky Way, though present-day OB-star catalogs yield conflicting rates (ranging from agreement to several times higher) so no rescaling of the ccSN map is performed.

title: An Optical Illusion: High Electron Densities Create Extremely Metal-Poor Galaxy Impostors
comment: 16 pages, 6 figures, submitted
summary: JWST has enabled the discovery of dozens of extremely metal-poor galaxies (EMPGs) with metallicities below $5\%\,Z_{\odot}$, representing a significant leap toward detecting the first galaxies without metals. However, accurate metallicity measurements require careful determination of physical conditions in the ionized gas. In this paper, we study four galaxies that appear to be EMPGs when analyzed using the direct $T_e$ method with the common low-density assumption ($n_e=10^3\,{\rm cm}^{-3}$). To test whether their metal-poor status holds when accurately measuring the density, we apply the direct method with a self-consistent determination of electron temperature ($T_e$) and density ($n_e$) in the high-ionization zone using the [OIII]$λ$5008, [OIII]$λ$4364, and [OIII]$λ$1666 lines, using JWST/NIRSpec data from the SPURS program in the Abell 2744 lensed field. We find that three out of four galaxies in our sample have extremely high electron densities ($n_e \sim 10^{5}-10^{6}\,{\rm cm^{-3}}$), which suppress the [OIII]$λ$5008 line and lead to underestimates of metallicity by up to $\sim1.1\,$dex when this density is not accounted for, and have true metallicities of 12+log(O/H) $\sim7.3-8.2$. Failure to account for high densities can therefore lead to systematic misclassification of metal-poor galaxies and biased conclusions about early chemical enrichment.

AI.tldr: JWST observations of four low-metallicity galaxy candidates reveal that three have extremely high electron densities (~10^5-10^6 cm^-3) that suppress [OIII] emission and cause metallicity underestimates by up to 1.1 dex, meaning their metal-poor status is largely an artifact of ignoring density effects.
AI.motivation: JWST has found dozens of extremely metal-poor galaxies (EMPGs) with metallicities below 5% Z_sun, which are key to detecting the earliest galaxy populations. However, accurate metallicity determination depends on correctly estimating physical conditions (Te and ne) in ionized gas. The authors aim to test whether galaxies classified as EMPGs using the standard low-density assumption hold up when a self-consistent density measurement is performed.
AI.method: Using JWST/NIRSpec data from the SPURS program in the Abell 2744 lensed field, the authors apply the direct Te method with self-consistent determination of both electron temperature and density in the high-ionization zone, using the [OIII]λ5008, [OIII]λ4364, and [OIII]λ1666 emission lines for four EMPG candidates.
AI.result: Three of the four galaxies have extremely high electron densities (ne ~ 10^5-10^6 cm^-3), which suppress the [OIII]λ5008 line. When this density is properly accounted for, metallicities are underestimated by up to ~1.1 dex under the low-density assumption. The true metallicities are 12+log(O/H) ~ 7.3-8.2, not within the EMPG regime.
AI.conclusion: Failing to account for high electron densities can lead to systematic misclassification of galaxies as extremely metal-poor, biasing conclusions about early chemical enrichment. Density measurements must be incorporated into direct-method metallicity analyses to avoid this systematic error.
